title: Managing Agent Permissions at Scale
summary: Azure caps a subscription at 5,000 role assignments and will not raise it. The quota ceilings, propagation delays and review mechanics that decide how many agents you can actually govern.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**The thing that stops a growing agent fleet is not judgment. It is arithmetic, and the numbers are published.** Azure supports up to 5,000 role assignments per subscription and Microsoft's own documentation says that limit "is fixed and cannot be increased". A Google Cloud allow policy holds 1,500 principals. An AWS managed policy stops at 6,144 characters and a role accepts 20 of them by default.


Grant one bespoke identity and one bespoke policy per agent and you can compute, today, the agent count at which your provisioning starts returning` RoleAssignmentLimitExceeded` . Nobody in that conversation will have made a bad security decision.


The usual framing says the problem at scale is consistency, and templates fix it. Templates do help, and NIST documented the reason they eventually stop helping twenty years ago: pushing per-request context into static roles produces roles "that are ad hoc and limited in membership, leading to what is often termed 'role explosion'".


We are not arguing against templates. We are arguing that a template is a source artifact, not an enforcement point, and that the enforcement points have ceilings, propagation delays and review mechanics you have to design around.


What to do this week: count your assignments against each provider's published quota, move per-agent grants onto groups so one assignment covers many principals, and turn on the usage reports that already exist. Google's IAM recommender compares granted permissions against the last 90 days of use, and AWS reports unused roles and unused actions without you writing anything.
